title: How do you answer "What else could the client do?" in a case?
description: Even open questions are structuring questions in disguise. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Answer "What else could the client do?" with a mini-structure: ask for a moment, name two or three buckets, put two or three specific ideas in each, then say which idea you would do first and why. Interviewers want ideas, but they also want order and judgement. A random list of ten ideas scores worse than six well-grouped ones with a clear priority.
body:
Stage 8 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why brainstorming is a structuring question

Open questions like "How could the client grow?" or "What could they do about it?" feel like a test of creativity. They are, partly. But they are also structuring questions in disguise. The interviewer is checking whether you can generate ideas that cover the ground, group them sensibly and pick the best one. The common mistake is listing ideas in the order they occur to you, with no priority.

The method

1. Take a moment

"May I take a few seconds to organise my ideas?" Twenty seconds of silence produces a far better answer than an immediate stream.

2. Pick your buckets

Choose a split that fits the question. Some that work almost anywhere:

  • Internal vs external (what we control vs the market)
  • Short term vs long term
  • Revenue vs cost
  • Today's capabilities vs new capabilities
  • Existing customers vs new customers

If your mind goes blank, one of these will get you started. There are more in how to create brainstorming buckets quickly.

3. Fill each bucket with specific ideas

Two or three per bucket is plenty. Make each one concrete enough to act on: "charge higher menu prices on the delivery apps" beats "look at pricing". Keep one good idea in reserve for when the interviewer asks "Anything else?"

4. Prioritise

Finish by choosing. Rank ideas on the client's actual objective, and on cost, speed and risk. "I'd start with the price change, because it is quick to test and has the biggest impact" is the sentence that turns a list into a recommendation.

A worked example

In the Coastal Brew case, a coffee chain's profit has fallen because delivery orders, after a 30% app commission, earn much less than café visits. The interviewer asks how the client could restore profit.

"I'd think about this in three buckets. First, make delivery orders more profitable: charge higher menu prices on the apps, negotiate the commission down in return for volume, and build a delivery menu around high-margin items with cheaper packaging. Second, move customers to cheaper channels: our own app with click-and-collect, which pays no commission, plus loyalty points to make the switch worthwhile. Third, fix the base: check staff rotas against the lower café footfall. I'd start with app pricing, because it's quick to test and we can size it now."

Then size the priority idea if you can. A delivery order is a $9.00 ticket. A 15% price rise makes it $10.35, of which the app takes 30%, $3.11. After $2.25 of ingredients and $0.90 of packaging, the order now contributes about $4.10, up from $3.15. If the apps expect 10% of the 2.7M yearly orders to be lost, 2.43M orders × $4.10 ≈ $9.95M, against 2.7M × $3.15 ≈ $8.5M before. That is a gain of about $1.45M a year.

Prioritising when ideas do not have numbers

Sometimes you cannot size ideas, but you can still compare them. A city asks how to cut bus delays. Ideas might include more buses, dedicated bus lanes, timetable changes and faster boarding. Group them by capacity, road priority and operating process.

Then compare them on the criteria that matter: likely minutes saved, cost, time to implement and effects on other road users. A dedicated lane may cut journey times most, but takes road space from cars. Extra buses cost more and do not fix congestion. Faster boarding, such as contactless payment at every door, is cheap and quick. A strong answer might start with boarding and pilot one bus lane on the worst corridor.

Add one real example

Tagging an idea with something you have seen in the real world makes an answer memorable: "Retention offers just before a contract ends work well; mobile operators do this when customers become free to switch." Use it once, not for every idea. See how to build business judgement for ways to collect examples.

Common mistakes

  • A random list. Name the buckets before the ideas.
  • Vague ideas. "Improve marketing" is a category, not an idea.
  • No priority. Always end by saying which idea you would do first, and why.
  • Ignoring the goal. Ideas that do not move the client's target belong at the bottom.
  • Running dry on "Anything else?" Keep one idea in reserve.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. "What could the client do to retain customers?" Open your answer.

Show a strong answer

"Let me think about this in two buckets: things we can do with today's products and team, and things that need new capabilities. On the first..."

Why it works: Buckets first, then ideas, then a priority.

2. A gym chain wants more revenue per member. Give three ideas in two buckets and a priority.

Show a strong answer

"Two buckets: charge more for what we already offer, and sell new things. In the first, a premium tier with off-peak class booking, and a modest price rise for new joiners only. In the second, personal training packages. I'd start with the new-joiner price rise, because it doesn't upset existing members and we can test it in a few sites."

Why it works: Grouped, specific and prioritised with a reason.

3. The interviewer asks, "Anything else?"

Show a strong answer

Bring out your reserve idea and place it in a bucket: "One more in the second bucket: corporate memberships sold through employers."

Why it works: It shows you had more and keeps your structure intact.

Where to practise next

Read the full guide to structured brainstorming, then do quick reps with the structuring drill. The next stage is delivering a 60-second recommendation.
